Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty.
  • Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.
  • Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

According to recent reports, the Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management.".

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:.

Recent findings suggest that the OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

Sources indicate that for existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:.

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Sources indicate that under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:.

According to recent reports, the difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

It has been revealed that the Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:.

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

Industry observers note that for now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:.

Sources indicate that both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

Industry News: Tech investor Bill Gurley says workers who went through the ‘college conveyor belt’ and chased safe jobs are at high risk of AI automation

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that professionals have taught for generations that succeeding in school and attending an elite university would guarantee a rewarding six-figure career.
  • Now, venture capitalist Bill Gurley cautions workers against blindly following the career blueprint.
  • “This is fresh and fast, and it’s attacking jobs that haven’t been attacked in the past,” Gurley stated during the On with Kara Swisher podcast earlier this year.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that professionals have taught for generations that succeeding in school and attending an elite university would guarantee a rewarding six-figure career. But within a matter of years, AI has disrupted the world of work, and it’s promptly taking over the office roles humans were once promised.

Now, venture capitalist Bill Gurley cautions workers against blindly following the career blueprint.

“This is fresh and fast, and it’s attacking jobs that haven’t been attacked in the past,” Gurley stated during the On with Kara Swisher podcast earlier this year. “It’s creating a lot of anxiety, but I don’t know that we can put it back in the bottle.”.

In a recent development, the prolific tech financier, famous for his early investments in Uber and Zillow, is skeptical the government could pass AI regulation or pull off a massive reskilling effort. So as the technology continues to automate traditionally stable and lucrative roles, like lawyers and software engineers, it’s imperative workers actually be invested in their profession—or risk facing the chopping block.

It has been revealed that “The people that are most at risk are the ones that are sitting idly in the job and don’t really have a why or a purpose for it,” Gurley mentioned. “A lot of the people that go through that college conveyor belt, that are chasing a safe job, that end up working as a widget or a cog in an industry they may not love—I think they are ripe for disruption.”.

The Benchmark Capital general partner acknowledges it’s easier noted than done, but the best strategy is to “craft your own career path” and tailor it to an individual’s distinct skills.

For those who can’t switch sectors or become self-employed, AI can act as career “jet fuel” that can make them even better at their jobs and indispensable to their employers.

According to recent reports, “If it’s out of your control, I just would say understand what it’s capable of in your industry and be the most AI-aware person in your job,” Gurley advised. “You’re going to then be the last person that they want to get rid of.”.

Gurley explores the idea that chasing a career of passion is a strategic edge, and not fluffy advice, in his newest book Runnin’ Down a Dream. He’s also one of several business leaders questioning the efficacy of how young professionals are trained to approach college.

The investor has noticed a few worrying trends that may inhibit young professionals from following their true aspirations, hurting their career success. Gurley explained that kids today are “programmed from a time perspective” more than other generations. The budding talent start worrying about having a stacked résumé from a young age, and now some colleges require students to apply with a major in mind.

Sources indicate that these restraints don’t allow them to freely explore what jobs they’d enjoy, instead funneling them into a professional path very promptly. He believes that’s part of the reason why so many people are checked out at work—a group that’s most susceptible to disruption.

Industry observers note that “There seems to me to be somewhat of a problem out there in that people aren’t landing where they’re passionate about what they’re doing,” Gurley said. “I don’t think it’s anyone’s fault, but I think we’ve turned the college matriculation process into this pressure cooker.”.

Former LinkedIn CEO Ryan Roslansky echoes some of Gurley’s philosophy about career success in the AI era. Workers won’t be able to simply coast on a glitzy Ivy League degree: They need to have passion for their professions and the necessary tech skills to succeed in their careers.

“My guess is that the future of work belongs not anymore to the people that have the fanciest degrees or went to the best colleges,” Roslansky said during a fireside chat at the platform’s San Francisco office last year.

Instead, he predicted talent most likely to land a job and succeed are “the people who are adaptable, forward thinking, ready to learn, and ready to embrace these tools…It really kind of opens up the playing field in a way that I think we’ve never seen before.”.

Fei-Fei Li, a Stanford professor and CEO of AI startup World Labs, dubbed the “Godmother of AI,” indicates being tech-savvy on the job matters more than anything else.

Now it’s essential for professionals to “superpower” themselves quickly with the tools, she advised.

A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on March 3, 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the UK Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) on Nov. 18 with seven recommendations on the draft documents CP26/36 and GC26/7. Three of them concern CP26/36, and four concern GC26/7. The letter was signed by HPC chief executive Jake Chervinsky.

According to recent reports, the UK's new crypto regime will start to apply on Oct. 25, 2027. The FCA opened its window for crypto license applications on Sept. 30, 2026, and the window will close on Feb. 28, 2027.

According to the letter, "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity." HPC argued that attaching obligations to a person who could not discharge them "would offer consumers no additional protection.".

It has been revealed that in the letter, HPC also compared public blockchains with the internet. "Like a public blockchain, the internet depends on protocols that identifiable persons maintain and upgrade over time," the group wrote.

It has been revealed that HPC asked the FCA to assess each participant in a blockchain network separately. Proprietary traders and market makers "supply much of the liquidity on which order books depend," the group wrote. HPC also asked the regulator to describe compliance requirements as outcomes and to hold regulated firms accountable for them.

On Aug. 24, HPC urged the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) to harmonize their rules for perpetual contracts. The group argued that such products should be classified by their economic structure. According to HPC, a harmonized framework would let exchanges compete on "execution quality and liquidity.".

On Sept. 30, HPC sent its response to the European Union's review of the MiCA rules. In it, the group asked the EU to treat crypto perpetual futures as derivatives under MiFID II. "Clarity in application, rather than new legislation, is what would assist in regulating perpetual futures," HPC wrote at the time.

Chervinsky previously served as chief policy officer at the Blockchain Association and as chief legal officer at the crypto venture firm Variant.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through.
  • I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI stocks have sold off and oil prices are lower, but the 10-year yield is at 4.94% and mortgage rates are still abouve 7.30%. So what gives?

Recent findings suggest that the Federal Reserve has been worried about oil prices driving inflation since the Iran conflict began and has noted that the trade war inflation has mostly been passed through. Now AI stocks are being slammed, with moratoriums on data centers coming in the near future as the anti-AI backlash grows. In this environment, you could expect the 10-year yield and rates to fall, but that’s not what’s happening.

I talked about this on the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor-in-Chief Sarah Wheeler, but with today’s market action, I need to revisit this question with some charts. Let’s go over each part of this storyline.

Industry observers note that oil prices were very volatile earlier this year and bond yields started moving in synch with them — especially after the first MOU deal broke off. Now that oil prices have fallen, you might expect at least a few Federal Reserve members to say that this could be a positive, but they haven’t.

In fact, when oil was trading between $68-$82, no Fed members said anything positive, and Cleveland Fed President (and Fed hawk) Beth Hammack talked about how lower oil prices were were actually bad for inflation because people could then spend more money.

In any case, so far, lower oil prices haven’t helped the 10-year yield get below 4.70%. If oil can trade between $67-$82, that would help a lot, but the last time that happened was when we confirmed a deal with Iran in June.

Sources indicate that I have used the CoreWeave stock price as an example of the problems with the AI companies. Since CoreWeave had some financing concerns, the markets have soured on AI, and as you can see in the chart below, the company’s stock price has been crushed. This has helped keep the 10-year yield below 5.35% for sure and has assisted in lower yields this week. But we are still elevated versus what we saw after the MOU deal was unveiled.

The Fed has made AI a huge inflation talking point, and they need to see much more pain in the AI sector before changing their tune.

If we were getting all this news about AI and oil prices four weeks ago, I believe the 10-year yield and mortgage rates would be lower today. But all this stock drama and falling oil prices came in a 14-day period where the Fed hawks came out every day talking about more Fed rate hikes, even a 50-basis-point hike. I mean, look at how the U.S. dollar hasn’t been fazed by the market drama.

Sources indicate that for the past two months, I have focused on two key levels for the 10-year yield: 5.35% and 5.15%. Both those levels held and yields have fallen from these points. So what lower oil prices and falling stocks have done is made sure bond yields don’t go much higher and for now, let’s take that as a victory. However, I do understand why people might be scratching their heads on why rates aren’t lower with lower oil prices and falling AI stocks.

The Fed hawks are the main reason bond yields aren’t lower; they want to make sure that the bond market doesn’t get relaxed, even with lower oil prices and falling stocks, and they have done their job well. They really want to take back all the insurance interest rate cuts from last year and because of this, the 10-year yield is still at 4.95%. If the Fed members weren’t so hawkish over the last two weeks, bond yields would be lower and we would have already had sub-7% mortgage rates.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.
  • That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am.

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” stated Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

According to recent reports, “Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom noted, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”.

Industry observers note that the panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn noted.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We demonstrated up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

Recent findings suggest that “The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she mentioned. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Recent findings suggest that fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

Recent findings suggest that “We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith remarked.

Industry observers note that the region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she stated. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn stated, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”.

#76250. Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier.
  • Recent findings suggest that we believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries.
  • companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:50 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante, Amit Eyal Govrin and John Furrier.

Recent findings suggest that we believe sovereignty is becoming an architectural requirement for firms operating globally, especially in highly regulated industries. The business question for buyers is how much control an organization needs over the systems that produce its intelligence, and what happens when that control is ceded to others.

U.S. companies supply most of the cloud and frontier artificial intelligence technology enterprises depend on. Buyers need to understand the resulting jurisdictional, operating and commercial risks, and put in place compensating controls to mitigate them. This reality applies for U.S. firms operating abroad and even those in the US, especially for regulated firms.

Welcome to Breaking Analysis #334: Sovereign AI: Where control becomes an architectural requirement.

In this episode we examine the issues around where data lives, who holds the keys, which model touches the data, who operates the system and who is exposed to the bill. Our premise is that sovereignty requires deliberate risk decisions, compensating controls and proof that those controls work. The appropriate architecture involves tradeoffs and will depend on the workload and the consequences of losing control.

Today we draw on three sources of input as shown below:.

Sources indicate that first, Amit Govrin’s buyer’s guide, which evaluates the documented controls across hyperscaler offerings and buyer territories. Second, a study we commissioned with our partners at Qualitate that brings the experiences of eleven senior technology decision-makers in regulated and critical-infrastructure organizations. Third, John Furrier’s conversation with Amit at SC26, which explains the reasoning behind our framework.

The buyer’s guide independently measures vendors’ documented claims. The in-depth interviews show what buyers care about and what they’ve tested. theCUBE interview helps connect those findings to architecture and business risk. The survey sample is small but deep, so we use it to understand decisions and expose gaps.

Let’s start by hearing from Amit with why he developed a practical and uniform framework to measure organizational control over AI, data and local risk:.

The first set of takeaways from our survey shows a gap between buyer priorities and operational reality. Legal exposures featured prominently in purchasing decisions within the sample. Yet seven of eleven respondents report no testing of disconnected systems, key-revocation or exit scenarios. So the hard evidence for practical operational control is somewhat shaky given the high levels of concern about losing that very control.

As shown below, buyers also tend to add controls to the platforms they already use. Only four of eleven have deployed or piloted a distinct sovereign or dedicated offering. Cost and the burden of adding another environment was the primary reason that explained such behavior.

As seen in the quote above, a European information technology and telecom buyer states deep support escalations “can still in some cases involve personnel or systems outside the EU, particularly for deep technical problems.” What’s the message there? Our take is that the support protocol must become a fundamental part of the architecture review; and that has to account for emergency and privileged access. The key point as Amit often stresses is sovereignty is not a purity test. Organizations can certainly live with such an exposure during an emergency. Our message is simply be aware of the condition, evaluate the risk and if necessary put in compensating controls or live with the exposure.

Recent findings suggest that it’s early days, so some customers are waiting for clearer sovereign-specific mandates or enforcement guidelines from local governments before expanding deployment and testing sovereignty. In other words, they’re leaning on existing privacy and cybersecurity laws and practices. We’d caution, however, that this type of uncertainty only strengthens the case for preparing acceptance tests sooner rather than later.

Costs heavily influence the scope of sovereignty investments. Buyers justify stronger controls for sensitive workloads while accepting different levels of exposure for lower-risk activity. Migration effort, retraining and the cost of exiting all affect that decision. At the very least, this means customers should assess their sovereign exposure, much in the same way they would do so for cybersecurity.

AI inference introduces another gotcha. Nine of 11 respondents require inference inside the sovereign or regional boundary. Buyers report that model availability can lag inside those environments. As such, the architectural choice has to make a potential tradeoff between local jurisdiction risk and model capability for a specific workload. The question buyers are asking: Is it worth stepping outside the lines to get a business result? The answer depends on the degree of risk and the magnitude of the business value. Sometimes it’s worth just paying the parking fine.

We’re not going to go deep into the buyer’s guide – we did that last week and we’d encourage you to read the full report.

What we will share is one high-level comparison from the buyer’s guide as shown below.

Recent findings suggest that google LLC leads all measured cloud vendors with a score of 3.45 across all regions and tests. Google is followed by Oracle Corp. at 3.25. IBM Corp. and Microsoft Corp.’s Azure score 3.0. AWS scores 2.7 – its score suffers from not having the ability to have a customer-run air-gapped stack without vendor management. Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd. and Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. came in at 1.2.

Now to be clear, this is a point-in-time index from the Nov. 14 revision. It averages each supplier’s best live offering across five buyer regions. The framework has five pillars (territorial, legal, operational, technical and financial), 17 yes-or-no tests across four nonlegal dimensions, plus a separate legal evaluation.

It has been revealed that as well, a low score at the highest level doesn’t mean a vendor won’t be chosen. We found many situations, for example, where Amazon Web Services Inc. was the choice despite its lower score because of its excellent quality and incumbent position. We found similar dynamics with Azure as a ubiquitous cloud and often a convenient option. Similar dynamics are in play within IBM and Oracle customer bases.

Sources indicate that that remarked, we’re assessing the architecture and the vendor claims to help buyers make better decisions. Customer-run deployments generally improve the scores because the methodology rewards controls the buyer can exercise independently. Missing documentation also affects the grades. We would use the previous chart to start an evaluation, then examine the actual offering available in the buyer’s jurisdiction against your specific workload requirements and local laws.

These findings bring us back to five key questions:.

Industry observers note that listen below to John and Amit connect operational controls and money flows to sovereignty. Those dependencies extend well beyond the physical location of the data center.

Let’s dig into some more survey data.

Seven of eleven buyers say a locally incorporated subsidiary does not completely clarify the local jurisdiction question. This is a buyer assessment, and it suggests the need for much deeper legal analysis beyond technical evaluations.

Under the U.S. CLOUD Act, a vendor subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be required to produce data in its possession or control, regardless of storage location. Corporate relationships and actual control do matter here.

Sources indicate that customer-held keys may limit outside access, but key ownership does not necessarily ensure legal immunity. Buyers also need to know what stops working if and when access is revoked.

The fuzzy gap is captured by a South American bank’s executive director for AI, talking about the absence of testing: “That’s probably the weakest point in our whole sovereign story.” Our takeaway is that legal review and operational testing serve different purposes and both are critical.

Recent findings suggest that coming back to the AI inference matter. As we showed earlier, nine of 11 buyers require inference to take place inside their sovereign or regional boundary. One Latin American financial-services buyer mentioned: “If it calls out to a U.S. endpoint, it doesn’t count no matter what the contract says.”.

In a recent development, this means you have to trace the end-to-end request cycle, from prompt, retrieval, model usage, outputs and even logs. An application that gets green lit can still depend on another service which lives in the execution sequence. The test is what happens to the data during its actual use.

Sources indicate that for sensitive workflows, buyers should compare a self-hosted open-weight model architecture with an approved frontier service and evaluate the cost and quality of the outcome. Open weights create optionality but the frontier often produces superior results which may warrant easing up on sovereignty requirements.

Sovereignty needs ongoing attention because the architecture changes continuously. A model endpoint can move, a newly introduced model ships, a service contract changes or a new capability goes into production. Every change can affect exposure and risk.

It has been revealed that in this clip, Amit describes an AI-driven five-pillar framework for continuous assessment and management of data sovereignty and third-party risk. The approach brings vendor capabilities and claims, and the customer’s architecture, into an ongoing assessment. Let’s hear how he puts it:.

According to recent reports, we see tremendous value in this framework. Our test for any assessment comes down to the evidence it produces. In other words, what’s the exposure, who has control, is there an accountable owner and ultimately, what’s the risk you’re absorbing? Our advice is that major changes to models, services or contracts should trigger a reassessment. Documented assurance from the vendor combined with technical tests should both be included in that process.

Our recommendation is to make sovereignty evaluations at the workload level. Start with a core business process, identify the exposures and agree on the controls it requires based on the risk you’re willing to absorb. Importantly, for critical workloads, we suggest obtaining proof that those controls work in a safe sandbox environment and then push into production.

Sources indicate that this means you have to pay attention to privileged access. And you must test what happens when a key gets revoked and you have to recover. As we’ve talked about in previous episodes, verifying what the model did and the route of the execution path is something most organizations can’t observe today. Testing and telemetry are major gaps with most customers. Can you observe the route and exercise an exit or completely disconnected scenario if a workload requires it? Your financial assessment should include ongoing operation, migration, retraining, the cost of leaving and business disruption. And importantly, a business owner has to accept the risk, not an IT pro.

For vendors, we believe the opportunity is substantial to document controls, establish predictable operating economics and provide credible evidence that can support your proposed solution. In many cases we’ve seen public documentation and evidence lack marketing claims.

According to recent reports, sovereignty is becoming part of enterprise architecture because intelligence now depends on these relationships. Buyers need the ability to make an informed choice and demonstrate that the resulting system behaves as intended.

According to recent reports, ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin believes younger generations investing in stocks and digital assets instead of housing could help ease pressure on property prices. However, he says crypto still needs something that makes housing attractive: stability.

Recent findings suggest that buterin thinks that housing creates incentives for owners to keep property prices high, even when cheaper homes would benefit society. Digital assets could offer an alternative, but today’s platforms often encourage excessive speculation.

“We need the equivalent of those good properties that housing investment has, for modern digital assets,” Buterin wrote on X.

According to recent reports, his comments raise a question for Ethereum. Can the network evolve beyond speculative trading and become dependable infrastructure for people building long-term digital wealth?

One benefit of younger generations investing more in stonks and other digital things instead of housing is that it reduces perverse incentives that drive people to push to keep housing expensive, instead of rejoicing when prices drop as we do for all other life necessities.That….

It has been revealed that ethereum’s development roadmap increasingly focuses on making the network faster, more efficient, and harder to disrupt. Its next major upgrade, Glamsterdam, is in testing, and ethereum.org lists a mainnet launch for Q4 2026 with no date confirmed yet. The upgrade introduces several changes designed to improve Ethereum’s capacity without sacrificing decentralization.

In a recent development, one major feature is Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS). It moves the relationship between block proposers and builders directly into Ethereum’s protocol, reducing reliance on external relays and additional trust assumptions.

Another notable development is Block-Level Access Lists. The feature prepares Ethereum to process unrelated transactions in parallel rather than handling everything sequentially.

These improvements could help Ethereum support more financial applications while keeping its infrastructure accessible to independent node operators. So, if digital assets are expected to become long-term financial instruments rather than vehicles for short-term speculation, this is very much needed.

Recent findings suggest that ethereum also provides an established foundation for staking, stablecoins, decentralized lending, and tokenized real-world assets. These applications could give investors more ways to hold and use digital wealth without constantly trading volatile tokens.

Yet, security, reliable applications, and responsible financial products must develop alongside network capacity.

Ethereum has several pieces of that foundation already, including proof-of-stake security, smart contracts, and an expanding financial ecosystem.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, more bad news for job seekers—especially non-grad Gen Zers.
  • When major employers like Google, Microsoft, IBM, and Apple all eliminated their long-held degree requirements for jobs, other firms rushed to follow their example.
  • Recent findings suggest that goodwill’s CEO Steve Preston told Fortune that while most CEOs have good intentions, they can’t control every interview or job offer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, more bad news for job seekers—especially non-grad Gen Zers. Just because an employer claims it’s ditching degree requirements to recruit more diverse talent, that doesn’t mean its hiring managers are actually doing it.

When major employers like Google, Microsoft, IBM, and Apple all eliminated their long-held degree requirements for jobs, other firms rushed to follow their example. But that promise may be limited to their job ads.

Recent findings suggest that goodwill’s CEO Steve Preston told Fortune that while most CEOs have good intentions, they can’t control every interview or job offer. And so the promise of skills-first hiring may not be reaching the millions of jobless Gen Zers who need it.

Recent findings suggest that “Right now, employers are consistently saying they want to hire for skills, not necessarily degrees,” Preston remarked. “But the proof is in the pudding. Not everybody does it.”.

He added: “What I hear from a lot of people is, ‘Yeah, the top says we need to do this,’ but when it gets to the hiring professionals, it doesn’t always trickle down.”.

The charity has more than 650 job centers and saw nearly 2 million people use its employment services last year, and Preston mentioned he’s preparing for an influx of jobless Gen Zers thanks to automation.

While the opportunities for young people without degrees are certainly growing, Preston states they’re ultimately still more likely to face unemployment than Gen Zers with a degree.

Sources indicate that “What I’m seeing is, of the overall unemployment, people without college degrees have no jobs,” the 66-year-old CEO, who formerly served as the 14th United States secretary of housing and urban development, revealed. Research has shown that the concern is even more acute for young men.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s much harder to find a job,” Preston added. “It’s really hitting college students right now in the marketplace. It’s really hitting young adults without college degrees.”.

So why are hiring managers still shutting the door on people who didn’t go down the higher education path, despite such a clear push to do the opposite?

“I think when somebody comes out with a four-year degree from college, there’s a certain sense that that person has a foundation that will be valuable in the workplace, and there’s a suspicion that if somebody hasn’t done that, they may be lacking some core skills,” Preston remarked, while pointing to critical thinking, team building, and communications as potential skills built from school projects and essays.

“So somebody with a strong collegiate background provides a high degree of comfort that these other capabilities are in place,” he added.

Sources indicate that “It’s also just easy to interview people who are like you, if you went to college, if you’ve gone down a particular pathway, you speak the same language, you have many of the same experiences. It’s much easier to connect with somebody who’s like you.”.

For young people without degrees, Preston argued the key is proving you’ve built those prized skills elsewhere—whether that’s through upskilling, volunteering, or work experience. Even joining a sports team can help open doors because it teaches you confidence, teamwork, discipline, and more.

“Employers have to be able to see that many of those capabilities are acquired in different ways,” he noted.

For closed-minded employers, Preston stressed the research is clear: Inclusive hiring isn’t just the right thing to do, it’s also good for business.

Sources indicate that “Organizations that have a much broader aperture in looking for talent are more likely to have the roles in their organizations filled; they’re much less likely to say that they’ve got deficiencies in their team; they’re more likely to say they’ve got a healthy workplace; and they often find higher engagement scores among their teams because of the culture that they’ve created,” he added. “Honestly, I think that’s crucial for society as well, on many levels.”.

A version of this story originally published on Fortune.com on September 26, 2025.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • exchange and the app highlights the balance.
  • Industry observers note that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app highlights the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Industry observers note that under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

According to recent reports, the Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

It has been revealed that for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

Industry observers note that for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Industry observers note that under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

Recent findings suggest that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

Sources indicate that the pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

  • 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- When does a business need a Fractional CIO?
  • Recent findings suggest that the HelloNation article explains that technology decisions often become more complicated as a business grows.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lionel Fermin examines when growing businesses may need technology leadership for planning, security, spending, and long-term technology decisions.

HOBBS, N.M., Nov. 21, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- When does a business need a Fractional CIO? A HelloNation article featuring insights from Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin of GlobaTech Solutions in Hobbs, Upcoming Mexico, explains when businesses may benefit from experienced technology leadership.

Recent findings suggest that the HelloNation article explains that technology decisions often become more complicated as a business grows. Fresh employees, software, equipment, and security risks can create challenges that basic technical support may not address. At that point, business leaders may need broader guidance about how technology supports the organization.

It has been revealed that the article describes a Fractional CIO as someone who provides technology leadership without serving as a full-time executive. While technical support typically focuses on fixing problems and keeping systems working, this role considers how technology decisions affect employees, customers, security, costs, and future business needs.

This broader perspective can become notable when several technology projects compete for attention. The article notes that businesses may recognize the need for improvements without knowing which ones should come first. Fractional CIO services can help prioritize projects according to risk, cost, and business value.

Technology planning is another major part of the role. Instead of waiting for systems or equipment to fail, the article explains that companies can prepare for equipment replacements, software changes, security improvements, and growth. Identifying major expenses early can also give leaders more time to compare options and prepare budgets.

Cybersecurity can create another need for technology leadership. The article notes that a security incident can interrupt operations, create financial losses, and affect customer relationships. Executive technology guidance can help leaders understand cybersecurity risks in business terms and determine which concerns deserve the most attention.

According to recent reports, the article also describes how Fractional CIO services can assist with customer or industry security requirements. Businesses may receive questionnaires or requests to demonstrate specific protections. Technology leadership can help identify gaps, organize responses, and provide a clearer view of existing security practices.

Growth can also signal the need for more structured technology guidance. Systems that worked for a small team may become strained as a manufacturer adds employees. The article explains that a technology strategy can help businesses prepare for greater demands on software, networks, security, and employee access.

Vendor management is another area where stronger oversight may be useful. Companies often work with separate providers for software, internet service, phones, security, and technical support. The article notes that reviewing vendor costs, contracts, performance, and responsibilities can help reduce duplication and clarify who handles vital technology needs.

According to recent reports, major business changes can also increase the need for planning. Opening a new office, replacing software, or hiring many employees may require coordination among leadership, employees, vendors, and technical teams. Managed IT Expert Lionel Fermin's insights featured in the article address how technology leadership can help keep these decisions connected to broader firm goals.

The article notes that not every company needs a full-time technology executive. Smaller businesses may instead need experienced guidance for certain projects or a limited number of hours. Warning signs can include rising technology costs, repeated cybersecurity concerns, unsuccessful projects, or leaders spending too much time managing technology questions.

In a recent development, A lack of shared planning may provide another warning sign. When departments make separate technology decisions, businesses can face higher costs, security gaps, and software problems. The article explains that a shared technology strategy can provide clearer direction across the organization.

In a recent development, ultimately, the article explains that the value of a Fractional CIO centers on planning and leadership rather than daily troubleshooting. Strong technology guidance can help businesses organize decisions about systems, security, spending, growth, and long-term needs.

When a Business Needs a Fractional CIO features insights from Lionel Fermin, Managed IT Expert of Hobbs, Latest Mexico, in HelloNation.

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm.

Jeff Bezos has a space organization, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder noted he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios declared Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos noted a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”.

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

Industry observers note that “We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”.

Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to recent reports, according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

Sources indicate that zecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

In a recent development, at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a newly introduced transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

In a recent development, the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

It has been revealed that ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

It has been revealed that as of ZecStats' latest enhancement on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

Industry observers note that in practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

Sources indicate that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

Recent findings suggest that that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

It has been revealed that every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (360 w)

Gonka AI Hit by $1 Million Exploit as Hacker Drains Stablecoins

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (360 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) network Gonka AI has reportedly suffered a massive security attack in which hackers exploited its Ethereum bridge to withdraw stablecoins and problem unbacked tokens worth over $1 million.
  • According to blockchain analytics firm Onchain Lens, the hacker was able to gain access to the bridge's BLS group key, allowing the attacker to withdraw funds and concern Wrapped Gonka (WGNK) tokens without backing them with the required assets.
  • Per the report, the hacker managed to withdraw $884,800 in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) stablecoins and also issued $172,000 in unbacked WGNK tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Decentralized artificial intelligence (AI) network Gonka AI has reportedly suffered a massive security attack in which hackers exploited its Ethereum bridge to withdraw stablecoins and problem unbacked tokens worth over $1 million.

According to blockchain analytics firm Onchain Lens, the hacker was able to gain access to the bridge's BLS group key, allowing the attacker to withdraw funds and concern Wrapped Gonka (WGNK) tokens without backing them with the required assets.

Per the report, the hacker managed to withdraw $884,800 in Tether (USDT) and USD Coin (USDC) stablecoins and also issued $172,000 in unbacked WGNK tokens.

Combined, the total value of the affected assets stood at around $1.06 million, per Onchain Lens.

Following the hack, the funds were transferred through the decentralized exchange Uniswap and multiple crypto wallets, making it challenging to trace their final destination.

The attack targeted Gonka AI's cross-chain bridge. The cross-chain bridge makes it possible to transfer assets from Gonka AI's native chain to Ethereum and vice versa.

According to the project's technical documentation, withdrawing funds from Gonka to Ethereum requires certain cryptographic signatures from the network's validator set.

The cryptographic signatures are checked against the BLS group key, which changes with every network epoch.

Per the report, the attacker was able to change the epoch BLS group key on the bridge, making it possible for the hacker to control the part of the bridge responsible for authorizing fund withdrawals.

Thus, the hacker was able to withdraw funds from the bridge's stablecoin reserves and glitch WGNK tokens without locking the required amount of assets on the native blockchain.

Blockchain security firm Blockaid noted that the hack had taken place, with the total amount of funds stolen reaching about $1.05 million across roughly five transactions at the time of the initial alert.

At the time it spotted the suspicious activity, Blockaid noted that the hack was still ongoing.

Onchain Lens's numbers differ slightly, with the firm reporting around $884,800 in stablecoin withdrawals and $172,000 in unbacked WGNK issuance.

Notably, the issuance of unbacked tokens presents an additional problem, given that such tokens could potentially enter circulation without the necessary reserves to back them.

Coinbase is bringing crypto trading directly into ChatGPT as competition for AI-powered financial services intensifies. Meanwhile, PancakeSwap has dropped “Swap” from its name, expanding beyond decentralized trading. The two developments show how Coinbase and Binance-linked crypto projects are positioning themselves for the next phase of digital finance.

It has been revealed that coinbase confirmed its ChatGPT integration yesterday, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The timing coincides with Pancake’s attempt to reposition itself beyond its original decentralized exchange business.

The Coinbase plugin allows eligible owners to trade crypto and equities without leaving ChatGPT. Users can request market or limit orders through conversational instructions.

Before execution, ChatGPT displays an interactive confirmation card showing order details. People must approve the transaction before Coinbase processes it through its Advanced Trade platform. Standard trading fees, eligibility requirements, and account limits still apply.

Sources indicate that coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single….

The integration also builds on Coinbase’s AI infrastructure. Its Coinbase for Agents toolkit provides developers with connections to trading accounts and market data. The ChatGPT launch brings those capabilities into a more accessible consumer interface.

Industry observers note that as of today, the official integration presently remains limited to eligible U.S. Coinbase consumers. It also depends on ChatGPT account and workspace availability.

Recent findings suggest that while Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how users perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform confirmed its rebrand today. The newly introduced identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Pancake now operates across more than 11 blockchain networks. The platform reports over 208 million customers and more than $4.4 trillion in cumulative trading volume.

It has been revealed that its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

Recent findings suggest that the rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Released in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

In a recent development, its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

Sources indicate that these agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

Sources indicate that this creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The S&P 500 closed Friday in a correction, falling 3.59% to 6,918.45 for its seventh straight loss and its longest losing streak since February 2020. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.28% and is now down more than 2% for the year. Goldman Sachs notes the index is 12% below its Oct. 6 record, and its strategists have named the three things they’d need to see before calling a bottom.

Snider’s note noted the sell-off “expanded this week from an AI unwind to a broader growth downgrade,” noting that the S&P 500 excluding AI had held up until this week and is now 6% below its high. Goldman’s AI stock basket is down 32% since Oct. 6. Cyclical stocks have lagged defensives by 5 percentage points over the past 10 days.

Goldman’s note was written before Friday’s rout was fully in its data. Its exhibits are priced as of Nov. 19 and its hedge fund data run through that date. So the question is whether Friday supplied what the note was looking for — the situation could be even worse in markets than it acknowledged.

Goldman mentioned any one of the following would support a bottom and a recovery: news that raises confidence in AI earnings, a dovish Fed signal, or a significant drop in investor positioning.

Condition 1: AI earnings. This is the one the market is trying to test. Investor Dan Niles told CNBC that a price war between Anthropic and OpenAI is hurting both, noting their combined sequential revenue growth fell from 75% in the second quarter to 48% in the third, while combined losses rose from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion. Reuters cited a valuation of about 40 times trailing sales for Anthropic. A US Bank Asset Management executive remarked the valuation “assumes years of rapid growth.” Goldman’s own outlook claims the AI outlook for 2028 and beyond “is highly uncertain.”.

Condition 2: the Fed. Futures put the odds of a December hike at about 95%, and the Fed meets Dec. 9. Goldman’s economists expect hikes in December and March, sending the federal funds rate to a peak of 4.25% to 4.5%. A dovish signal looks unlikely soon. Treasuries did rally sharply Friday as investors looked for safety, which is not the same as a Fed pivot. Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said Thursday that the Fed will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high. The 10-year Treasury yield is near 5%.

Sources indicate that condition 3: A major drop in investor positioning. This has often marked the end of past drawdowns.

Sources indicate that the first condition is unsettled, to say the least. Anthropic’s historic IPO turned into a sort of referendum on the entire AI trade, an unfair weight to put on a single, albeit remarkably vital, manufacturer. The company raised $93.5 billion after underwriters exercised an option, passing SpaceX’s $85.7 billion as the biggest IPO on record. The shares jumped 17% on Thursday, then gave most of it back Friday to close at $88.91, not far above the $83 IPO price. “Anthropic faded relatively swiftly,” noted Dakota Wealth’s Robert Pavlik. “I don’t think investors believe there’s something inherently wrong with the company… I think they’re just skeptical of this market.” Morgan Stanley, the underwriter tasked with stabilizing the shares, closed its support position, removing a potential pillar of support.

Recent findings suggest that UBS stated the debate had shifted from whether AI investment will continue to whether it can generate enough revenue and returns for shareholders. A Capital Economics economist wrote that the IPO’s success while other AI stocks fell highlights the parts of the AI ecosystem “no longer move as one,” as chipmakers Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron and AMD fell roughly 12% to 14%.

In a recent development, nvidia’s 14% fall on Friday was its worst day in almost two years. It lost 22.9% on the week and is down 47.5% since Oct. 6, a loss of $2.7 trillion in market value. Reuters reported the SEC is probing its accounting practices. Jensen Huang resigned as CEO on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO. The VIX, Wall Street’s “Fear Gauge,” closed at 35.89, its highest in 19 months.

It has been revealed that “It’s a meltdown right now,” noted Arun Sundaram of CFRA Research. JPMorgan Asset Management’s David Kelly took the other view: “This is not a fatal illness. It’s not even the flu.”.

According to recent reports, on the third condition, Goldman’s note notes hedge funds have already cut back. Their net leverage is the lowest since April 2025. A companion report, Snider’s Hedge Fund Trend Monitor, says the most popular hedge fund longs were crowded into the AI trade and have lagged the S&P 500 by 14 percentage points over six months. That is among the worst stretches in the basket’s 20-year history. The note described the situation for hedge funds as “bruised and broadening.”.

But Goldman’s broader Sentiment Indicator is still above average. U.S. equity mutual funds and ETFs have taken in nearly $170 billion in the fourth quarter so far. Asset managers’ net equity futures positions are in the 82nd percentile of the past 10 years. Goldman’s equity strategists estimate the AI boom has lifted S&P 500 earnings 25% above trend. Goldman Research says AI capital spending produced “about half” of this year’s earnings growth.

Industry observers note that the Street is split on whether this is the top. Capital Economics expects further declines. Goldman’s Nov. 17 outlook, written before the drop, forecast 8,700 by the end of 2027. In the Nov. 20 note, its range runs from about 5,800 to 8,100 depending on whether investors regain confidence in earnings. From Friday’s close, that is roughly 16% downside and 17% upside. Those percentages are my math, not Goldman’s.

Industry observers note that after the 22 S&P 500 corrections since 1980, the index averaged a 4% return over the next three months. It rose in 17 of them. E*Trade’s research is less reassuring. Of the 14 times since 1983, the index first closed 10% or more below a record, five became bear markets.

💡 Key Takeaways
