  • In a recent development, sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion.
  • Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:00 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 7:47 am.

In a recent development, sila, a startup producing next-generation battery materials, announced a long-term customer agreement with Panasonic Energy Corporation of North America potentially worth more than $1 billion. To meet demand from Panasonic and other buyers, the company aims to expand its plant in Moses Lake, Wash., supporting roughly 500 additional manufacturing and construction jobs over the coming years.

Panasonic, a battery supplier to Tesla, will buy Sila’s Titan Silicon anode material for its U.S.-made battery cells. The silicon-carbon composite can replace some or all of the graphite in lithium-ion battery anodes to improve performance.

In a recent development, sila began operations at its Moses Lake plant last year and has about 100 full-time employees at the site. The facility is still scaling up production, with initial capacity designed to supply batteries totaling about 2 gigawatt-hours — enough for roughly 20,000 to 50,000 EVs, depending on how the material is used.

The expansion will increase that capacity to tens of gigawatt-hours, said Gene Berdichevsky, Sila’s co-founder and CEO.

“This is a really crucial blueprint for reindustrializing the U.S.,” he remarked. “We have to take new technology and leapfrog China, not just copy what they’ve done over the last 20 years.”.

While the U.S. has expanded battery manufacturing, it still depends heavily on overseas suppliers for core materials and technologies, Berdichevsky said. Sila aims to strengthen that domestic supply chain with higher-performing components.

Batteries support industries central to energy independence and national security. They power EVs, consumer devices, drones, robotics and hardware deployed in space, and provide backup electricity for data centers.

Berdichevsky noted Titan Silicon can help a battery store 20%–40% more energy in the same space, cut recharging time roughly in half and deliver more power than a battery using a conventional graphite anode. The anode itself is also much lighter and smaller.

Sources indicate that in August, Sila received a conditional federal loan commitment of up to $1.4 billion through the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital to expand domestic battery technology manufacturing. The company must meet financial, legal, technical and other requirements before the loan can be finalized.

It has been revealed that the startup previously received a $100 million grant during the Biden administration under a similar initiative to increase U.S. energy independence. Those funds helped build its plant in Washington.

The manufacturer has also raised $1.6 billion from private investors, including a $300 million round unveiled in July. The 15-year-old company is valued at $2.27 billion, according to PitchBook.

Industry observers note that seattle-area startup Group14 also makes a silicon-carbon anode material. It operates a smaller-scale manufacturing facility at its Woodinville, Wash., headquarters and produces commercial-scale volumes at a plant in South Korea.

Group14 has partially completed its Moses Lake manufacturing site but repeatedly delayed the start of production. It now targets mid-2027 to bring the first of two production units online, with no firm completion date for the second. It recently announced looks for a factory in Spain.

Growth is key to bringing down costs and making Sila’s technology competitive in mass-market batteries, Berdichevsky noted.

“This is really the beginning of chapter three for our company’s history,” he noted.

According to recent reports, the first two chapters were inventing the technology and moving from grams to tons of production, he added. This phase is about reaching the mass market. Sila aims to begin manufacturing at the expanded facility in 2028, with output increasing over time.

Industry observers note that “None of this is easy,” Berdichevsky noted. “It’s not the inventing technology; it’s the manufacturing of it that’s really really hard, and we’re going to try to more than 10x the scale from what we’ve already done.”.

  • Industry observers note that in his latest X post, CZ pointed to a Nov.
  • The recent call by Japanese authorities comes after a massive cybersecurity attack on a popular Japanese car-sharing service called Times Car, operated by Park24 Group.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, widely known as CZ, has expressed his concerns about the storage of sensitive personal data after Japanese authorities called on rental car services to delete customers' identity documents following a massive data breach.

Industry observers note that in his latest X post, CZ pointed to a Nov. 18 notice issued by Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC). The notice urges rental car services to be cautious about unnecessarily storing images of driver’s licenses and other government-issued identification documents.

The recent call by Japanese authorities comes after a massive cybersecurity attack on a popular Japanese car-sharing service called Times Car, operated by Park24 Group.

The incident began when the tech giant noticed suspicious activity on its system on Sept. 25. As a result, it launched an investigation into whether someone had accessed its systems without permission, potentially exposing customer data.

As per the disclosure by Park24 on Oct. 23, about 6.63 million customer accounts were impacted by the breach.

Worse, the investigation uncovered evidence that hackers had transmitted 1,464,800 encrypted images of identification documents, including driver’s licenses, to external locations.

According to recent reports, besides that, another 891,602 encrypted images of identification documents were accessed suspiciously. However, investigators found no evidence that these additional ID images had been transmitted outside the organization’s systems.

Industry observers note that japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission issued its notice on Nov. 18, focusing on the risks of retaining sensitive personal data even after its original purpose has been fulfilled.

The regulatory body stressed that storing unnecessary identification images could significantly worsen the consequences of cyberattacks.

Although Japan’s latest warning specifically targets the rental car industry, CZ’s decision to share his concerns about this concern also raises questions about personal data protection in the crypto industry.

Generally, centralized crypto exchanges require people to go through a Know Your Customer (KYC) process to access their trading platforms.

Depending on the platform and jurisdiction, these processes may require consumers to provide photos of their passports, driver’s licenses, national ID cards, and other sensitive information.

This kind of sensitive data can be a goldmine for cybercriminals, who can exploit stolen personal information for various activities such as identity theft, phishing attacks, fraudulent registrations, and more.

Only 18% of Gen Z workers want to build AI skills. A Wharton professor claims using AI is riskier for them

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The generation with the longest careers ahead of them appears to be the least interested in sharpening their AI skills, according to research from talent services firm Seramount released Thursday: Only 18% of Gen Z employees want to develop or improve their AI skills, compared with 36% of millennials, 46% of Gen Xers, and 43% of baby boomers.

For younger workers, using AI could come with a different set of professional risks than it does for their more experienced colleagues.

“Because younger workers haven’t had the same amount of time in their career fields to build up their standing as experts, using a technology that blurs their own contribution to their work can feel especially risky,” Jessica Reif, an assistant professor of management at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School, told Fortune.

The survey of more than 1,800 U.S. white-collar employees at companies with at least 500 workers, conducted in June through NORC’s AmeriSpeak panel, found that 58% of Gen Z employees use AI in their current roles, compared with 60% of baby boomers, 63% of millennials, and 67% of Gen Xers. Seramount defined Gen Z as workers 29 and younger.

That leaves a puzzle. Gen Z workers, often cast as digital natives, use AI at nearly the same rate as baby boomers but show far less interest in getting better at it.

Younger workers are considerably more concerned about what using AI might say about their own abilities.

Some 22% of Gen Z employees surveyed by Seramount worry that using AI could lead others to question their skills, compared with 10% of millennials and Gen Xers and just 8% of baby boomers. Only 27% of Gen Z employees feel comfortable acknowledging their use of AI for a work task, compared with between 47% and 53% of their older colleagues.

Industry observers note that those concerns are not entirely unfounded. In four experiments involving more than 4,400 participants, Reif, then at Duke University, and her co-authors Richard Larrick and Jack Soll found in a study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that employees described as receiving help from AI were perceived as less competent, less diligent, and lazier than those described as receiving other forms of help or whose use of help wasn’t specified.

According to recent reports, the stigma could also influence hiring decisions. In one experiment, managers who used AI less frequently themselves favored candidates who did not use AI, while managers who were more frequent AI consumers favored candidates who used it daily.

The penalty in those experiments held regardless of the age of the employee being evaluated. But Reif said its consequences could be more substantial for workers who are still trying to establish themselves professionally.

“A senior employee who uses AI has a more substantial record of results that can offset doubts about their effort or ability, but an early-career employee doesn’t have that record yet so others might weight their AI use more heavily when evaluating them,” Reif stated.

The pressure can work in the opposite direction, too. A survey of 3,001 professionals worldwide released Tuesday by the London School of Economics’ Inclusion Initiative and consulting firm Protiviti found that 48% of employees worry about being judged for not using AI enough at work, compared with 20% who worry about being judged for using it.

For workers at the beginning of their careers, that presents a dilemma: They need to demonstrate their ability to work with AI while also proving what they are capable of doing themselves.

Beyond concerns about their professional reputation, younger workers appear less convinced of the benefits of using AI in the first place.

In a recent development, only 30% of Gen Z employees in Seramount’s survey believe AI helps them work more efficiently, compared with roughly half of their older colleagues. And 41% believe it improves the quality of their work, compared with 56% of Gen Xers.

Young people are also questioning whether the immediate benefits of AI could come at the expense of their long-term development. A survey by Gallup, the Walton Family Foundation, and GSV Ventures of 1,572 Americans aged 14 to 29, released in April, found that 80% believe using AI tools is very or somewhat likely to make learning more difficult for them in the future.

Among employed Gen Z respondents, 48% believe the risks of AI in the workforce outweigh its benefits, compared with 15% who believe the opposite. Some 69% place greater trust in work completed without AI than in AI-assisted work.

That skepticism, as Fortune has reported, partly reflects how poorly schools, employers, and government have prepared young people for an AI economy.

Younger employees’ attitudes toward AI may also reflect the environments in which they are being asked to use it.

Only 27% of Gen Z respondents in Seramount’s survey stated their organization provides support to help them integrate AI into their work, compared with 38% of millennials and 43% of Gen Xers. Younger employees were also the least comfortable seeking help from colleagues on how to use AI tools, with only 18% saying they felt comfortable doing so, compared with 34% of baby boomers.

Seramount suggested that junior employees may also have less need for AI in their current roles or more limited access to enterprise AI tools.

The LSE and Protiviti research points to the importance of training in AI adoption across generations: 93% of employees who had received AI training used the technology at work, compared with 50% of those who had not.

Not all research suggests young workers are being left behind on training, though. The LSE and Protiviti study found that 66% of Gen Z employees had received AI training in the past year, compared with 40% of baby boomers. That study polled professionals worldwide, while Seramount surveyed only U.S. workers.

For employers, failing to engage their youngest employees in AI adoption could create a longer-term talent development problem, echoing warnings that automating entry-level roles could cost companies their future workforce.

“If Gen Z falls behind on AI, employers risk weakening their future leadership pipeline,” Diana Forster, senior director of research at Seramount, mentioned in a press release. She called on employers to provide clearer guidelines, training, and opportunities for young employees to practice using the technology.

Despite the challenges young workers face in embracing AI, the technological disruption could also work in their favor.

According to recent reports, openAI CEO Sam Altman believes that periods of rapid technological change give people at the beginning of their careers a chance to gain a competitive advantage. As AI transforms how jobs are done and opens up upcoming business opportunities, those with fresh ideas and new skills could have an edge over more established players.

“I think you want to start your career at a time of the greatest change, when the playing field is most open,” Altman said during an interview with Stanford’s Graduate School of Business in October, as previously reported by Fortune.

He added, “I think people with high potential, drive, ideas, a new way of looking at things, and new skills tend to do relatively well when the ground is shaking the most.”.

For workers concerned about being judged for using AI, Reif offered some advice.

It has been revealed that “No matter their age, employees are increasingly in a position where they need to demonstrate their value above and beyond what AI can do,” Reif mentioned. “Employees who are proactive in communicating how AI enables them to contribute more or in ways that would not have otherwise been possible may be able to counteract some of these perceptions.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift.
  • In a recent development, “We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:28 EST / NOVEMBER 21 2026.

AI spending is shifting from giant training clusters toward smaller, promptly built sites, and modular data centers are becoming a natural home for inference workloads. Power, cooling and memory supply now shape where tokens get generated as much as raw chip performance does.

Inference-first chipmakers want to capture that shift. Positron AI Inc., which raised $875 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, builds inference appliances around commodity memory instead of scarce high-bandwidth memory. Inference has overtaken training as the force behind infrastructure buying decisions, according to Cameron McCaskill (pictured), head of sales and business development at Positron.

In a recent development, “We’re at a point where about two-thirds of the workloads being run through these AI infrastructures are inference versus one-third is training. And back in 2023, it was like 85% training, 15% inference,” McCaskill said. “So now you can see why inference is driving the economic decisions of how they’re going to build out their infrastructure.”.

McCaskill spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed inference overtaking training, Positron’s commodity-memory chip design and why low-power modular data centers suit inference. (* Disclosure below.).

Sources indicate that positron’s first-generation Atlas server ran on a programmable chip, and the company looks to tape out its own silicon early next year for its Titan server. Oracle Corp. is bringing about 340 Atlas servers live in its cloud this quarter, McCaskill noted. A neocloud provider has also signed on for Atlas and committed to Titan. Positron’s central design choice was skipping high-bandwidth memory.

“Everyone else pretty much in the industry is using what’s called HBM or high bandwidth memory. It’s very limited in supply, very expensive,” McCaskill mentioned. “We went with commodity memory.”.

Sources indicate that that choice also keeps power low enough for air-cooled rooms. A single Positron server draws about 4,500 watts, and a full rack of Titan servers fits within 40 kilowatts, McCaskill explained. That footprint suits sites where operators can find a few megawatts of cheap power without heavy regulatory hurdles. For inference providers monetizing new capacity, deployment speed is a big part of the appeal, according to McCaskill.

Recent findings suggest that “One of the groups of companies that we’re seeing a rise in right now and coming to us for product is these modular data centers, where they have a half megawatt or, 1 megawatt or 2.5 megawatt modular data center, and those can be deployed very swiftly,” McCaskill remarked. “And the goal of a lot of these inference players is I want to get from land and power to monetizable tokens within 90 to 120 days. And those modular data centers, coupled with our technology, can be a great solution.”.

#76233. Industry News: Can AI Hack Smart Contracts? How AI Agents Are Changing Blockchain Security

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (715 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 U ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Can AI Hack Smart Contracts? How AI Agents Are Changing Blockchain Security

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: U

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smart contract vulnerability scanners typically work by looking for certain patterns.
  • For example, in December 2025, Anthropic released results from SCONE-bench, a smart contract benchmark of 405 contracts that were exploited in the 2020 - 2025 period.
  • To make sure the agent was not simply memorising exploits that were already published, newer vulnerabilities that had been published after their training cutoff were tested on Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5, which were able to generate $4.6 million (simulated stolen funds).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smart contract vulnerability scanners typically work by looking for certain patterns. However, because an AI agent can iterate and make use of dependencies, local blockchain forks, and decompilation, it weakens the protection gained by keeping source code secret, and can attempt attacks against complex vulnerabilities such as access control bugs, accounting errors, oracle-related bugs and unexpected contract interactions.

For example, in December 2025, Anthropic released results from SCONE-bench, a smart contract benchmark of 405 contracts that were exploited in the 2020 - 2025 period. They were able to reproduce exploits for 207 contracts, totalling $550.1 million (simulated stolen funds).

To make sure the agent was not simply memorising exploits that were already published, newer vulnerabilities that had been published after their training cutoff were tested on Claude Opus 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, and GPT-5, which were able to generate $4.6 million (simulated stolen funds).

Finally, they analysed 2,849 recent smart contracts with no known complications, discovering two previously unknown vulnerabilities that could have resulted in $3,694 (simulated stolen funds), emphasising the ability of AI agents to discover newly introduced vulnerabilities rather than simply exploiting known ones.

According to recent reports, anthropic emphasised that no actual funds were lost during these experiments. It should also be noted that in one of their experiments using GPT-5, it cost $3,476 for API usage, which leaves a slim (simulated) profit.

Industry observers note that with automated hacking becoming more effective, how can we be sure that DeFi will be able to stay ahead of these AI agents? Hacken, a blockchain security firm, reported that $1.18 billion was lost in 107 crypto hacks during the third quarter of 2026. 48% of this was from exploiting smart contracts.

In a recent development, of course, this doesn’t specify the cause of these hacks. Regardless, it emphasises the importance of being able to stay ahead of AIs which could be used for exploitation.

Industry observers note that chainalysis estimates that approximately $36.7 million was stolen in 2026 from DeFi protocols that had not undergone smart contract verification. It also notes AI-assisted reverse engineering as an emerging risk without attributing any particular thefts to AI.

In an experiment by a16z on 20 past DeFi price manipulation exploits, apparent success rates of 50% were reduced to 10% when the researchers restricted access to transactional data that revealed the original exploit. When the researchers gave the AI some high-level information about the DeFi domain, success rates jumped to 70%.

In February 2026, OpenAI and Paradigm released a benchmark for evaluating agents’ abilities in the domains of vulnerability detection, patching, and exploitation using an EVM environment (EVMbench). Results showed that GPT-5.3-Codex achieved a 71% success rate in exploitation (limited to a sandboxed environment) and 33.3% for GPT-5.

In October 2026, CyberChainBench was released, analyzing 541 exploit events across 9 Ethereum-compatible blockchains. The best-performing configuration achieved 37.5%, 43.7%, and 23.4% success rates for detection, exploitation, and patching respectively.

Industry observers note that in a simulation, the best-performing agent profited $57.4 million from exploits on 200 exploit events that occurred after the cutoff. Some of the reported high-severity issues were evaluated and determined to not be exploitable by OpenZeppelin. Since much of the data is trained on in the public, results may be exaggerated.

In a recent development, agents will continue to improve, and while current results are not an indication that AI-driven agents are responsible for large scale on-chain thefts, it is an indication that AI can find and exploit weaknesses in smart contracts given a certain environment. Given the ease with which agents can try attacking many different protocols, smaller protocols may see an uptick in exploit attempts.

Industry observers note that teams that implement rigorous testing and monitoring could have an edge over other teams. For example, AI could be used to test a contract prior to deployment, generate regression tests, and identify weird behavior on-chain. A human would still need to verify any potential challenges and sign off on changes.

Teams should continue to perform third-party audits and implement other security best practices such as limiting access to sensitive information, setting up alerts and response prepares, restricting the amount of money in a wallet, making sure AI systems do not have permissions to transact without human oversight where necessary, and so on.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ahmed Barakat is a journalist and copywriter based in Georgia with a growing focus on blockchain technology, DeFi, AI, privacy, digital assets, and fintech innovation.

It has been revealed that the CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Industry observers note that another day, another security scare. This time, Etherscan is warning users after detecting attempts to gain unauthorized access to its customer support system. But the timing could hardly be worse for an industry already dealing with a growing list of cyberattacks.

The warning comes just days after hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely, injecting malicious code into websites operated by 178 organizations. The affected names included HSBC, BBC, Ledger, IKEA, Salesforce, Zoom, and CNN.

Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, crypto platforms have faced separate attacks involving compromised API keys, protocol vulnerabilities, and stolen customer information. Traditional banking has not escaped either, with a French bank recently losing approximately €100 million to hackers.

It has been revealed that so what kind of security era are we entering? The problem is no longer confined to crypto exchanges or experimental DeFi protocols. Banks, technology companies, payment providers and blockchain businesses are increasingly exposed to the same interconnected digital infrastructure.

Industry observers note that etherscan disclosed earlier today that attackers had attempted to gain unauthorized access to its Freshworks customer support and ticketing system. The company is investigating and has introduced precautionary measures. It has not confirmed that customer records were successfully accessed, but warned users about suspicious support communications, unexpected links, and requests for sensitive information.

Security Notice: Reminder Regarding Etherscan Support CommunicationsEarlier today, we detected attempts to gain unauthorized access to our customer support and ticketing system (Freshworks).We are currently investigating the situation and taking precautionary measures.In….

Recent findings suggest that the concern is particularly relevant because support impersonation remains an effective way to steal owners’ crypto and money. An attacker posing as an Etherscan representative could exploit a user’s existing support request to make a phishing message appear legitimate.

Industry observers note that but Etherscan is hardly the only name facing security questions this week. Just two days ago, hackers exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation signup process. They injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects, allowing the code to run on websites using the affected software.

Optimizely confirmed the vulnerability and stated it had removed the injected code and fixed the flaw. Its November 17 incident report said the unauthorized party exploited the signup process rather than stealing customer administrator passwords.

The financial damage remains unclear. It is reported that investigators could not establish how many visitors were affected or whether the attempted thefts succeeded.

The uncomfortable takeaway is that attackers did not need to breach 178 separate companies. They exploited one software provider whose code was embedded across hundreds of websites.

According to recent reports, crypto’s security problems extend beyond Etherscan and the Optimizely incident. DeFiLlama’s hack tracker recorded several attacks during the week, including a $10.39 million incident involving Lighter Perps on November 16. The attacker exploited a compromised trader API key, enabling unauthorized withdrawals.

Lighter noted its protocol and smart contracts were not compromised. It temporarily suspended withdrawals and activated Guardian mode to prevent further unauthorized activity.

Recent findings suggest that another incident hit MORE Markets, where an attacker exploited a lending mechanism to drain approximately $308,000 in WFLOW. B18 TimeBank also suffered an exploit on November 17, losing $404,540 in USDC through its reward voucher redemption mechanism.

According to recent reports, these incidents show different weaknesses across crypto infrastructure. Not every loss comes from a broken smart contract. Compromised credentials, vulnerable applications and flawed authorization mechanisms can be equally damaging.

Industry observers note that traditional finance faces its own problems. French lender Crédit Mutuel Arkéa disclosed a cyber heist earlier in November, with hackers stealing approximately €100 million through fraudulent transactions originating from the bank’s own accounts. The bank remarked customer assets were not affected, although some transactions were temporarily suspended.

Deutsche Bank also made headlines on November 17 after confidential internal documents surfaced through an international journalistic investigation. It was a document leak, not a confirmed breach of its current banking systems.

Recent findings suggest that deutsche Bank said security testing found no indication that its current IT environment, account information, login credentials, or payment data had been compromised. Still, the leak could have wider geopolitical repercussions.

Banking institutions are not immune to major security incidents simply because they operate under traditional financial regulations.

Crypto has suffered enormous losses. The October Binance incident alone involved $6.3 billion in stolen digital assets, making it one of the largest cryptocurrency heists on record. Yet, traditional finance also faces attacks involving payment infrastructure, third-party service providers, and internal transaction systems.

It has been revealed that the Optimizely incident is particularly revealing. Both HSBC and Ledger appeared among the affected organizations. The vulnerability did not care whether visitors were interacting with a traditional financial institution or a crypto company.

Neither system offers complete protection. The real question is whether companies can secure the increasingly complex infrastructure connecting their services. A single compromised vendor can expose hundreds of organizations, while one stolen credential can bypass otherwise sophisticated security systems.

Crypto owners have every reason to demand stronger protections. But traditional banking customers should not mistake regulation and familiar branding for immunity.

With Etherscan investigating attempted unauthorized access, the data provider is now joining the growing list of companies dealing with security incidents.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.
  • Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle firm talked about building for years but always found too major to take on.
  • The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 8:57 amNovember 18, 2026 at 9:01 am.

Cloud-infrastructure startup Pulumi has a name for its current fiscal year, which started in July: “the year of absurd ambition.” The first results arrived Wednesday: two products the Seattle firm talked about building for years but always found too major to take on.

The products, Pulumi Delivery and Pulumi Agents, let AI agents take over more of the work of getting fresh software up and running, and fixing it when something breaks.

“The ceiling on what we can accomplish is no longer limited by the speed at which we can build software,” said Joe Duffy, the firm’s co-founder and CEO, recounting the message he delivered to the Pulumi team. “It’s limited by how ambitious we’re willing to be and how big we’re willing to dream.”.

The ambition is all the more notable because Pulumi is getting smaller. The company has about 100 employees, down from about 130 last year. Duffy mentioned there were no layoffs, and that AI has changed people’s roles and made the company more efficient.

Annual recurring revenue per employee more than doubled over the past year, he said. The company isn’t profitable yet, but it has had a few months of positive cash flow this year. Pulumi hasn’t raised money since 2023, when it landed a $41 million round led by Madrona, bringing its total to about $99 million over the company’s lifetime.

Recent findings suggest that pulumi’s co-founders include Duffy and Eric Rudder, both Microsoft veterans. They started the company in 2017 to let engineers manage cloud infrastructure such as servers, networks and permissions by writing code in everyday languages like Python and TypeScript.

The latest products take that approach further:.

In a recent development, to decide whether a change is safe to ship, Pulumi Delivery can use Jev, an AI model from TypeSafe AI that estimates the odds of specific risks the team asks about in a planned change. If a risk is higher than the threshold the team sets, the release stops.

Duffy mentioned he first noticed TypeSafe in May when it signed up as a Pulumi customer, because he liked the name. A few months later, Jev took off and TypeSafe used Pulumi to expand worldwide.

It has been revealed that “Now even the call on whether a change ships can be made by a model,” mentioned Daniel Gafni, a member of the technical staff at TypeSafe AI, in the Pulumi announcement. “That’s exactly the kind of decision we built Jev to make.”.

Recent findings suggest that both products are available now in public preview. Some features, including Jev decision gates and setting up agents, require Pulumi’s paid Pro or Enterprise looks.

Lucky timing: Pulumi’s founding bet on everyday programming languages turned out to suit AI agents, which are trained to be very good at writing exactly that kind of code.

“I wish I could say I predicted that 10 years ago, but it turns out in this case, what’s good for humans is also good for agents,” Duffy said.

In a recent development, AI agents now handle 40% of the operations on the Pulumi platform that people used to do, up from 15% in April and none in January, Duffy noted. Agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Pulumi’s own Neo are making infrastructure changes on their own.

Duffy noted many companies building AI coding tools stop once the code is written and reviewed. “For them, life stops at the merge,” he said. The fresh products cover the steps after that, from testing through release.

Plenty of organization: Pulumi won’t have this market to itself. Duffy pointed to Harness, which calls it the “agentic SDLC” (short for software development lifecycle), and GitHub, which pitched “agentic software delivery” at its Universe conference last month. He stated Cursor aspires to solve the problem and Anthropic built its own internal system.

The new products could replace some of the work now done by tools such as Argo CD and GitHub Actions, along with lots of homegrown scripts, he said.

“This is an industry-changing moment, and somebody has to solve this problem,” Duffy remarked. “And I think we are exceptionally well poised to do so.”.

Bring your own bot: Neo, the infrastructure agent Pulumi introduced last year, is now just one example of a Pulumi agent. Customers can set up as many as they want, each with its own job, instructions and tools. They can also bring their own agent, such as Claude Code or Codex, and run it in Pulumi’s cloud.

Sources indicate that neo itself, which ran mainly on Anthropic’s Claude, can now use models from OpenAI or Google, too. “It’s not just Anthropic anymore,” Duffy noted.

Agents can start work from an alert in PagerDuty, Datadog or Honeycomb, on a schedule or on request, and they report back to teams in Slack.

Pulumi has briefed about 50 customers, and about a dozen are in a private beta. Duffy said no launch in the manufacturer’s history has gotten a warmer reception, and he named Moderna among the customers eager to get it.

Pulumi has thousands of customers overall, including major companies such as BMW, Snowflake and Wiz.

According to recent reports, the business: Pulumi’s gross margins have stayed in the high 80s to low 90s even as agents drive up usage, Duffy said. Many customers run Pulumi from inside their own Claude Code sessions, which means they’re paying both Anthropic and Pulumi.

Duffy remarked Pulumi wasn’t out looking for money when it raised its last two rounds. Investors came to the firm, and each deal came together in about 48 hours.

Madrona’s Tim Porter has joined the board, Duffy said, taking the seat previously held by the late Soma Somasegar, who led Pulumi’s first investment.

Industry observers note that about 40 of the company’s 100 employees are in the Seattle area, working out of an office at Two Union Square. Duffy said Pulumi is hiring more people locally because in-person work still matters when building latest products.

Despite the smaller headcount, Pulumi is still hiring, including sales reps in nearly every region of the world. Inside the manufacturer, Duffy noted Pulumi is having a lot of success with “product-minded engineers who can think from our customers’ point of view, who can think like engineering managers, commanding a team of agents.”.

Sources indicate that asked whether a sale or more funding was in the cards, Duffy mentioned Pulumi aspires to be a long-term successful business. “There are a variety of ways to get there,” he said. “But we want to get there on our own terms.”.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still claims Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

According to recent reports, circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Sources indicate that most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Industry observers note that embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle unveiled in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide states "message limits will tighten over time until no fresh burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Recent findings suggest that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the organization wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide claims "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

Sources indicate that the migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

Industry observers note that the main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

It has been revealed that circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

Industry observers note that as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small glitch, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Sources indicate that many developers now ask AI assistants to write or revision integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

Recent findings suggest that the fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

It has been revealed that for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

‘An extraordinary and extreme backstop’: Earthjustice warns Army off bypassing paused Iowa permit

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A federal appeals court has paused the emergency permit authorizing the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, in a notice filed on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency, government lawyers remarked they would oppose a motion by two environmental groups to keep the permit on hold.
  • Industry observers note that the notice did not say whether the Army prepares to go ahead with the detonation, now set for Monday, Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A federal appeals court has paused the emergency permit authorizing the U.S. Army to blow up nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa. But the Justice Department told the court Friday that the Army may be able to proceed without it.

According to recent reports, in a notice filed on behalf of the Environmental Protection Agency, government lawyers remarked they would oppose a motion by two environmental groups to keep the permit on hold. The notice added that “in qualifying emergency situations,” EPA regulations authorize the Army, which is not a party to the case, “to implement waste treatment activity without an EPA permit” when there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment.”.

Industry observers note that the notice did not say whether the Army prepares to go ahead with the detonation, now set for Monday, Nov. 23. An Army Sustainment Command spokesperson did not respond Friday when asked whether the Army would proceed while the stay is in place, the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported. On Friday evening, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds activated the State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate state, federal, and local agencies ahead of the planned blast.

Thien Chau, a senior attorney at Earthjustice, which represents the groups, called the emergency provision “an extraordinary and extreme backstop” and said the groups “strongly urge” the Army not to rely on it.

The standoff leaves residents of southeastern Iowa and western Illinois facing a weekend of uncertainty over whether a plume of lead-laden dust will drift across their towns and farmland on Monday.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit issued its order late Thursday, pausing the permit the EPA issued to the Army on Nov. 13 after finding the material posed an “imminent and substantial endangerment to human health and the environment.” The pause lasts until the court rules on the groups’ emergency motion, which asks it to keep the permit on hold while it decides the case. The government noted it would file its full response by Sunday.

Cody Smith, director of climate initiatives at the Iowa Environmental Council, one of the groups that filed the lawsuit, stated detonating without the court’s approval would be unlawful. The council and the Sierra Club Iowa Chapter argue that the permit lacks adequate protections for health and the environment, that the EPA did not fully consider alternatives, and that it was issued without the public notice and comment they say the rules require.

According to recent reports, hours before the court acted, the Army postponed the detonation from Friday to Monday. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle stated Monday was the “latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

According to recent reports, the 68 drums of lead azide, an explosive used to set off munitions, were stored on site for more than 20 years in a bath of ethanol and water. The Army notes the material degraded and recrystallized, leaving it highly sensitive to friction and shock.

The blast is expected to release a plume of dust containing lead. Army maps modeled for a Friday detonation projected the dust settling across a roughly 25-mile stretch north of the plant, with low levels of airborne lead traveling farther. The Army asked some residents of Middletown, a town of about 360, to leave their homes during the blast because it could shatter windows.

The permit required the Army to model the plume using conservative assumptions so as not to “under-predict” potential impacts, and it states that EPA and Army experts agree the modeling is “not necessarily representative of actual conditions.”.

The Army held a public open house about the planned detonation in mid-October. On Nov. 15, five days before the original blast date, it released the detonation date and plume maps, meeting the permit’s requirement to publish a preliminary forecast at least five days in advance.

Smith mentioned the council began receiving calls from concerned residents on Monday, Nov. 16, and when it contacted state and local officials, “We were telling them for the first time.” Reynolds’ office has said neither the governor nor any state agency was told of the prepares before the Army’s Nov. 15 announcement, Little Village reported.

“This lawsuit is largely the outcome of a last resort,” Smith said.

It has been revealed that A letter from the EPA paints a different picture. Writing to Reynolds on Friday, Jim Macy, who heads the EPA’s Region 7 office, mentioned the agency issued three emergency permits for the lead azide between April and September and notified Iowa’s congressional delegation, state lawmakers, and local officials each time, and again on Nov. 13 when it approved the detonation.

According to recent reports, illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Illinois Sens. Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth, and Iowa Sen.-elect Josh Turek were among a bipartisan group of officials who wrote to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin urging a delay. “We call on you to consider delaying this detonation until there is an opportunity to explore safer alternatives,” they wrote, according to CBS News.

Sources indicate that the Army’s environmental assessment considered chemical neutralization, which would avoid a blast plume, but rejected it. The assessment concluded that the 7 to 22 days of handling it would require created an unacceptable risk of a fatal accidental detonation, with no guarantee that neutralization would work.

Macy’s letter remarked the Army also weighed building a structure over the material, moving it to the plant’s open detonation unit, and leaving the drums in place, and found each posed “an unacceptable safety risk” because of “advanced crystallization.” The Army, he wrote, “concluded the only viable option was a controlled detonation in place with extensive mitigation measures.”.

The environmental groups say the Army chose detonation “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead.”.

“It’s not our role to recommend to the Army or the EPA how to deal with explosives most effectively,” Smith said. “As far as we can tell, it’s been stored on site for at least 20 years, and they’ve known about this for at least the last several months. And they decided to wait until the very last minute to glitch that permit and make it publicly known.”.

In September 2025, the Army posted a federal contracting notice saying it planned to have American Ordnance LLC, which operates the plant, perform “lead azide neutralization.” The notice did not describe the method. The Army’s environmental assessment says the material’s degradation was discovered in March 2026. The Army has not responded to requests for clarification about the notice.

Army spokesperson Justine Barati told Radio Iowa on Nov. 17 that residents worried about lead dust on their property had a simple remedy: “The good thing is, if people have concerns about it being on their property, all they have to do is hose that off, and it’s gone.” The station reported that fine lead particles could reach as far north as Maquoketa.

Smith remarked that advice, including the Army’s guidance to hose off playground equipment and wash cars, is inconsistent with how lead persists in the environment. The groups’ court filings called the idea that lead can be washed away “absurd, counterfactual, and extremely harmful misinformation to share with the public.” Iowa health officials say no safe level of lead exposure has been identified.

Sources indicate that in his letter, Macy said EPA staff have been in Middletown since Nov. 16 testing drinking water and watersheds, and that the EPA and Army will provide filters to homeowners on public water systems if testing finds elevated lead.

“People have really been scrambling for information about what to do,” Smith said.

Recent findings suggest that the court could rule before Monday. If it grants the groups’ motion, the permit stays on hold while the case proceeds. If it denies the motion, the pause ends and the Army is free to proceed under the permit. Whether the Army would invoke the emergency exception if the court rules against it remains an open question.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median.
  • Industry observers note that XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that XRP stands out as the cryptocurrency with the most alarming volatility warning among major digital assets, according to recent Coinbase data. The options market indicates that traders are now preparing for price swings that could be nearly double XRP's historical seven-day price move.

XRP's seven-day options-implied price move stands at 1.94 times its historical median. This figure far exceeds similar metrics for major cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH) and Solana (SOL).

Industry observers note that XRP exhibits the highest premium above its own historical volatility. Solana reveals the lowest premium among these four cryptocurrencies, Coinbase remarked.

As the chart below indicates, the options-implied seven-day price move for XRP is around 9.6%, according to Glassnode and Coinbase data as of Nov. 17. This compares to its historical median absolute price move of about 4.9%.

Basically, this means that the options market is signaling a price swing nearly twice as large as XRP's typical seven-day price movement.

According to recent reports, interestingly, Solana's implied price move is also close to 9.5%, almost the same as XRP's. Yet its historical median weekly price move is much higher at about 6.5%.

The key here is that although both cryptocurrencies exhibit similarly large potential price moves, the magnitude of the expected volatility surprise is significantly greater for XRP relative to its usual trading range.

It has been revealed that for comparison, Bitcoin demonstrates an options-implied seven-day move of about 6%, versus its historical median of about 3.5%. For Ethereum, these numbers are about 8% and 5.1%, respectively.

Industry observers note that obviously, this latest figure doesn't necessarily imply that XRP is going to crash. It's a sign that options traders expect a substantial price move regardless of its direction.

Implied volatility is a forward-looking measure. It's based on options prices. The higher the implied volatility, the more traders pay for exposure to potential price movements or protection against them.

It has been revealed that the chart from Coinbase is based on a one-standard-deviation estimate. It's derived by converting annualized at-the-money implied volatility into a seven-day timeframe.

For XRP, the roughly 9.6% implied move represents a statistical range. It's not a guaranteed price target. A one-standard-deviation range suggests about a 68% chance of the price staying within this range under typical modeling assumptions.

Thus, the latest figure of 1.94x implies that XRP's volatility premium remains high despite a slight decrease from the previous reading.

In a recent development, from XRP traders' perspective, this can be a very challenging market environment. For traders using leverage, there could be a high risk of liquidation due to potentially sharp price moves.

#76223. Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1205 w)

Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • In a recent development, for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale.
  • A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

Industry observers note that the same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Industry observers note that venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

It has been revealed that companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other. Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an key regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

Industry observers note that as an example, Pear Therapeutics revealed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off. This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

Industry observers note that early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction. A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Sources indicate that has the founder or manufacturer addressed these issues in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

These challenges make the earliest stages of firm formation particularly key. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

In a recent development, at Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the manufacturer is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

Sources indicate that that means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

It has been revealed that AI and newly introduced distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

It has been revealed that the traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

In a recent development, moving quickly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

According to recent reports, for investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a organization needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

It has been revealed that the most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

It has been revealed that for decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

According to recent reports, healthcare is the clearest example. A tech giant can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

Industry observers note that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

The summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

According to recent reports, proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration plan and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

In a recent development, the technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It shows how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository notes a yes vote does two things:.

It also indicates plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

Recent findings suggest that A no vote would stop the whole proposal. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Recent findings suggest that turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

It has been revealed that mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

Sources indicate that the tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC revealed almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

Industry observers note that the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Sources indicate that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

In a recent development, the spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

It has been revealed that at launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Sources indicate that proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence reveals what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

Recent findings suggest that the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the initiative goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The sketch spread across social media within days, largely because so many viewers saw their own families in it.
  • A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans, nearly 1 in 4 adults, had provided ongoing care in the past year to an adult or child with a medical condition or disability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that on the Nov. 14 episode of Saturday Night Live, host John Mulaney starred in a parody drug ad for “Sister,” “a live-in, 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free and also your sister.”.

The sketch spread across social media within days, largely because so many viewers saw their own families in it. Its jokes land on real pressure points in American caregiving: who does the work, what it costs them, and how much more of it is coming.

A 2025 report from AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving found that 63 million Americans, nearly 1 in 4 adults, had provided ongoing care in the past year to an adult or child with a medical condition or disability. That is 45% more caregivers than a decade earlier.

Sources indicate that the work has also gotten harder. More than 40% of caregivers provide high-intensity care, and more than half perform medical and nursing tasks such as giving injections and managing catheters. Only 22% have been trained to do them.

An aging population is the main driver, indicates Geoff Gross, founder and CEO of Medical Guardian, a Philadelphia-based medical alert and connected-care company. But strains on the broader care system are pushing more Americans into the role.

“What we’re also seeing is pressures on in-home care and labor overall,” Gross mentioned. “There’s a burden on caregivers right now that is not scalable.”.

Paid help is scarce and expensive. As gerontologists Jane Tavares and Marc Cohen wrote for Fortune, a home health aide runs a median of about $6,688 a month, while the direct care workforce remains underpaid and short-staffed.

The sketch opens with Mulaney’s character weighing a nursing home against a private aide who “could cost thousands a week.” For real families, the costs keep compounding long after the caregiving ends.

A report published Nov. 4 by the AARP Public Policy Institute modeled the lifetime income losses of working caregivers born between 1981 and 1985. The typical caregiver in that group stands to lose about $120,500 in earnings, workplace retirement income, and Social Security, including roughly $15,400 in retirement and Social Security income alone.

Sources indicate that across that single five-year birth cohort, the losses add up to an estimated $2.3 trillion. Only 3.4% of working caregivers in the model lost no work hours to care. Chandra Bozelko, who cares full-time for her parents, ran those numbers on her own family in a recent Fortune commentary.

For some, the strain reaches the basics. In the 2025 AARP survey, 1 in 5 caregivers stated they couldn’t afford necessities such as food.

The sketch’s sharpest line comes from a doctor, played by Mikey Day, who explains that “years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours.”.

Research from the University of Michigan published in October suggests the gap behind the joke is widening. If current rates hold, U.S. women can expect to spend seven years of their lives caring for older family members or friends, up from six in 2011. Men’s lifetime total held steady at four.

It has been revealed that the difference isn’t in caring for spouses, where men and women spend about the same time. It demonstrates up in care for parents and grandparents. Edward Jones managing partner Penny Pennington has called it “the elder daughter phenomenon,” arguing that eldest daughters are quietly propping up family finances.

“Women still bear disproportionate financial burden, time burden, and energy burden,” Gross noted, adding that any progress on the matter “isn’t happening fast enough.”.

It has been revealed that demand for care will only grow. The U.S. Census Bureau projects that in 2029, Americans 65 and older will outnumber those under 18.

“Caregiving is really a societal crisis, but it isn’t designated in that way as much as it should be compared to other things we read about each and every day,” Gross said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

The two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA stated.

In its latest update on the investigation, ULA said it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

On Tuesday, ULA remarked early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

Industry observers note that the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp said Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the tech giant looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

The finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Upcoming Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn debuts reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA said.

The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA remarked it will share more as the investigation continues.

#76217. Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1259 w)
